hints: Focus on what ethanolic NaOH does to a bromoalkane, elimination to form an alkene by removing HBr.
Look at 2-bromobutane first and count the different beta-carbons with hydrogens, C1 versus C3 give different alkene skeletons.
Check if the two branched bromoalkanes can form positional isomers or only the same 2-methylpropene, then pick the combination that gives more than one C4H8.
walkthrough:
**Recall the reaction condition**

Great start, ethanolic NaOH with heating means elimination, not substitution.

$$\text{R-CH}_2\text{-CHBr-R'} + \text{NaOH (ethanolic)} \rightarrow \text{alkene} + \text{NaBr} + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$
A hydrogen is removed from a carbon next to the C-Br carbon, a beta-carbon, to form C=C.

**Analyse compound 1**

2-bromobutane is $\text{CH}_3\text{-CHBr-CH}_2\text{-CH}_3$.
There are two different beta-carbons. Remove H from C1 gives but-1-ene, $\text{CH}_2\text{=CH-CH}_2\text{-CH}_3$. Remove H from C3 gives but-2-ene, $\text{CH}_3\text{-CH=CH-CH}_3$, which itself exists as cis and trans isomers. So 1 gives more than one product of formula $\text{C}_4\text{H}_8$.

**Analyse compound 2**

2-bromo-2-methylpropane is $(\text{CH}_3)_3\text{CBr}$.
All three methyl groups are identical. Removing any beta-H gives the same alkene, 2-methylpropene, $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{C=CH}_2$. So only one $\text{C}_4\text{H}_8$ product.

**Analyse compound 3**

1-bromo-2-methylpropane is $\text{BrCH}_2\text{-CH(CH}_3\text{)-CH}_3$.
The only beta-carbon with hydrogens is C2. Removing that H gives only 2-methylpropene, $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{C=CH}_2$. No positional isomer is possible. So only one $\text{C}_4\text{H}_8$ product.

**Conclude the combination**

Only 1 gives more than one $\text{C}_4\text{H}_8$ alkene. 2 and 3 each give a single alkene. That matches 1 only.

options.A: This means 1, 2 and 3 are all correct. 1 is correct but 2 and 3 are not, since both 2-bromo-2-methylpropane and 1-bromo-2-methylpropane can only eliminate to give 2-methylpropene.
options.B: This means 1 and 2 only are correct. 1 is correct, but 2 is a trap. The tertiary bromoalkane $(CH3)3CBr$ is symmetrical, all beta-hydrogens are equivalent, so only one alkene forms.
options.C: This means 2 and 3 only are correct. Both are incorrect. Each has only one distinct elimination pathway leading to the same product, 2-methylpropene, so neither gives more than one C4H8 isomer.
options.D: This means 1 only is correct. 2-bromobutane can eliminate in two directions to give but-1-ene and but-2-ene (cis plus trans), so more than one C4H8 product, while 2 and 3 give only 2-methylpropene.
